slides.headline: Van Gogh thought this painting was a failure
slides.sub: Vincent van Gogh, The Starry Night, 1889

slides.headline: Painted in an asylum
slides.text: In 1889 Van Gogh admitted himself to an asylum in Saint-Rémy, in southern France. This is the view from his window, before sunrise.

slides.headline: The village isn't really there
slides.text: He couldn't see a village like this from his window. He added it from imagination, and painted the picture by day, from memory.

slides.headline: A Dutch church in France
slides.text: The tall, pointed steeple looks more like a church from his native Netherlands than one from Provence.

slides.headline: The dark flame
slides.text: The cypress rises like a flame from earth to sky. In Mediterranean culture, cypresses grow in cemeteries and are linked with death.

slides.headline: This star is a planet
slides.text: The big bright star next to the cypress is most likely Venus. Van Gogh wrote to his brother that he had seen the morning star, looking very big.

slides.headline: The swirl
slides.text: The sky moves in great spirals. Real night skies don't look like this; it is how he felt them.

slides.headline: Moon and sun at once
slides.text: The crescent moon glows with a halo so strong it almost looks like a sun.

slides.headline: "Another failure"
slides.text: In a letter to a friend he called his attempt at painting stars too big a failure. Today it is one of the most recognised paintings in the world.
